title: Renée Vaugeois: What led to her decision to resign from the Edmonton Police Commission?
article: Renée Vaugeois, executive director of the John Humphrey Centre for Peace and Human Rights, stepped down last week from the Edmonton Police Commission following a third-party conflict-of-interest review. Her resignation came despite the commission voting to keep her on.
Vaugeois is the second commissioner to resign this year, following Dan Jones's departure in mid-January.
Vaugeois, who had served just five months, said she stepped away to protect the commission's work from being overshadowed. She spoke with Postmedia Thursday about the decision.
Q: How are you feeling after your resignation?

A: It was a very stressful week last week, a lot of tears leading up to the meeting with the commission. On Friday, after some conversations with folks at the commission, I just chose to step away. So I am really sad. I think I could have made a really positive contribution in this space and could have been a really strong supporter of the police service. I'm feeling a bit heavy about it.
Q: What led you to make that decision, especially after the commission voted to keep you on?

A: There were two things that pushed me there. One being the letters coming from the minister to the commission really indicated to me that, even though I went through this review and it was quite intensive and that I was clear of any concerns, there was going to be (consistently) stepping in on that issue. And from the chief's office perspective, there was discomfort in me being there, regardless of the commission voting me back in. There was always this fear, this reticence. Regardless of what I could contribute, the perception was going to inhibit good work.

The folks on that commission, there's an amazing crew of people, and the last thing they need is something like that overhanging them, because they've got big things to do this year, and for it to be continually overshadowed, like the fact that last week, a whole day had to be spent deliberating on whether to let me back in, because there's a fear how the chiefs are going to react, or how the minister is going to react, and so it's just not fair to them. They deserve to be able to do the work without this drama and politics over top of them. That's why I made the decision.
Q: What was your thought when the conflict-of-interest inquiry was launched?

A: The report from Veritas, actually, there was nothing concerning. I went through a couple interviews, I know they were sifting through my socials. There were no real problems there at all. That was only one reference in January by the former chief last year when Mathios Arkangelo was shot, I kind of hit a breakpoint. And I posted on social media and reposted stuff about rallies, and I posted when I was angry. I was angry about not only that Mathios was shot in broad daylight, but he was left to bleed on the street for 25 minutes. So there's real concerns about the process and things that happened.

But also, the Edmonton Police Service (EPS) is one of the leading police forces in this country, we had the first police constable in the country, we were one of the first to have a hate crimes unit. But there are spaces where we need to really be able to question or think about how we improve, not just in terms of how we work with the community, but also how we support police officers.

So last year, I posted a couple posts in frustration, and that's the only thing that was pointed out in the report from Veritas. But one thing I have learned is that while officers may get support internally, the community is kind of left grieving, and nobody's supporting them. And I felt like it was my responsibility last year, given my role in the community, to question what happened.
Q: Do you think your advocacy, particularly around homelessness and human rights, is incompatible with police oversight?

A: No, I don't. I'm not even on the board or a member anymore with the Coalition for Justice and Human Rights. Last year, they supported a litigation against the city that wasn't led by me, it wasn't decided by me. But I don't think it's incompatible, because it wasn't the police service that was the focus. It was about municipal bylaws and the encampment policies and how we're responding to folks on the street. There are ways that we could take more dignified approaches that aren't like seizing people's property, causing more trauma, and I don't think that's incompatible.

I actually think EPS, with their help unit, are trying to do things in a really good way, and they're making progress. My biggest concern about that is the funding for those units, it's based on external funding, so it's concerning to me that while we're trying to build these really good responses and help people navigate in the right way, it's not a long-term funded process. So I think those are the lenses I was bringing into the commission. I actually think I could have been a really constructive part of the conversation there and supported in a good way, because I think the value I brought to the commission was my connection with community.
Q: What message do you think your resignation sends to other community advocates who might want to engage in public oversight roles?

A: I think more people need to be willing to engage in those spaces and put their names forward. My concern is that me stepping away may result in people being even more apprehensive about putting their name forward. But if you look at some of the commissioners that are on the team, they are amazing people. But just because I had such a public face with human rights, I became more of a concern.

I think what I would tell the community is, don't let this pause you. I think it should inspire us to actually engage more. Because like I was mentioning, the people on that commission are wonderful. They are really intent on doing really good work. The trick is that they get hampered by some of the politics on the outside. I think we as a community should be supporting them and working with them to help understand and engage around the community perspective.

I just think that the role of the commission is misunderstood in the community, and I think there's a real deeper role of creating stronger community relations as well with the commission, so that they strengthen their legitimacy within the community lens. And I think that was my goal when I was going in there. We really need people who want to be there and who are ready to be there and to bring their energies to the space.
Q: Looking back, is there anything you would have done differently during your time as commissioner?

A: No, not at all. I only had five months so I didn't get to engage too much, but I think I built really great relationships with the team, and I wish them the best. I wouldn't do anything differently at all. I'm just really sad that I can't be there to support this journey ahead.
